title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
author: Steven Morris
text:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.

But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC) , has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.

“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field , said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate , about a century ago.

A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.

Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.

Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West , said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.

Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
author: Dara Kerr and Gabrielle Canon
text:
A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California .

The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.

But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable.

Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers.

This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county : rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost.

“I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.”

Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies.

With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions , Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return.

What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community .

Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects.

It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in.

“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”

When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both.

Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee.

Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models.

“We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district.

“We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement.…

title: The top five Yankees’ pitching performances of 2026
author: Matt Ferenchick
text:
It was a pretty good year for the rotation, so let’s look back at some of their best games.

While the 2026 Yankees season has come to a frustratingly early end, it’s hard to blame much of that on the starting pitching. By several measures, the Yankees had one of the best rotations in all of baseball this year, and they have the favorite for the AL Cy Young Award in Cam Schlittler.

As part of our season in review, let’s take a look back at some of the rotation’s best efforts of the year. To do that, we’re going to rank them according to the Game Score statistic . Game Score takes a variety of stats from an outing and combines them to try and determine how dominant a pitcher’s outing. Fifty is generally about average, and if a pitcher nears 100, they’re probably putting up an all-time great outing. While we didn’t get any no-hitters or perfect games this year, the Yankees’ rotation still had its fair share of excellent outings, let’s look back at the best of them.

This is a post of the top five, but there was a three-way tie for fifth, so it’ll actually include two bonus games too.

One could hope that Schlittler’s Game 2 start in the ALDS against the Rays harkened back to a regular season outing he had against Tampa Bay. Facing the Rays on July 6th, Schlittler allowed one run on four hits, while striking out eight in eight innings. None of the hits he allowed were more than a single, it’s just that one of them was to the speedy Chandler Simpson, which led to him scoring on another single.

Sneaking onto the list as part of that three-way tie for fifth is, surprise, another Schlittler start. This is the only game on the list that the Yankees ended up losing, but you can hardly blame that on the Yankees’ Cy Young candidate. In his seven frames, he held Atlanta to one run on three hits while striking out 11. Thankfully the Yankees scored a run in the eighth and the loss came in extra innings, so Schlittler didn’t get dinged with a loss for that gem.

You’ll never be able to guess who the pitcher who had the other game tied for fifth is…

While it wasn’t as statistically dominant as his start against the Red Sox in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler’s 2026 outing was still plenty good enough to crack this list. He only went 6.1 innings this time around, but held the Red Sox to just two hits, while striking out 10. The Yankees’ lineup poured it on late on route to a win and an eventual dominant sweep of Boston. If only the rest of the postseason went that well…

Someone else has finally made an appearance on the list. Injuries limited Fried to just 112.2 innings this season, but statistically he was still very good. This performance against the Red Sox was part of that. Having been given a 3-0 lead to work with after the top of the first, Fried proceeded to go eight scoreless innings, allowing just three hits and two walks, striking out nine Boston batters.

Normal service has resumed as Schlittler matched Fried to tie for third place. However, this was another game where he ended up with a no decision thanks to the offense. In eight innings, Schlittler held the Angels to one run on two hits, striking out nine. The only issue was that one of those hits was a Vaughn Grissom homer that tied the game at one in the seventh inning. The Yankees eventually broke through with five runs in the top of the 10th inning to seal the win, although they deprived their ace of the victory.

As it turned out, there was also a tie for first and, yes, Schlittler was involved. In July, he held a potentially very powerful Phillies’ lineup to no runs in 7.1 innings, surrendering just three hits all game. He struck out 12 batters, including Trea Turner and Bryce Harper twice each.

Tying Schlittler for the top spot is a Rodón start that had people wondering what order the playoff rotation should go in. Against the Rays in late September, Rodón threw eight shutout frames, allowing just three hits in arguably his best ever start as a Yankee. He also reached a milestone in getting to the 1500 strikeout mark during the outing.

The start — and his stretch run in general — was good enough that it led to people suggesting that Rodón should get the ball for one of the AL Wild Card Series games. In the end, they went with Schlittler, Fried, and Gerrit Cole had their been a Game 3. As it worked out, Rodón didn’t end up pitching at all in the playoffs. You can debate whether that should’ve been the case, but it’s hard to blame any of the starting pitchers for their ALDS losses.

Those are the best starts of the year according to Game Score, but which ones were the most memorably good to you?

title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
author: Emma Roth
text:
OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.

OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.

Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?

In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak , suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.

Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup , raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”

Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August . Amazon has since filed an amended complaint .

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems

This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon , which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok , Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.

“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge . “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”

Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month . “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.

The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”

The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.

While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

title: Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
author: John Higgins
text:
Wired earbuds are making a small comeback, and Bose is capitalizing on it — with ANC this time.

After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of decline.

Part of the resurgence can be tied to the fact that they’re cool now with younger generations — following the revival of tape decks and vinyl. Celebrities have been spotted wearing them , and there’s even an Instagram account that follows the trend. Wired earbuds have real benefits. They don’t need a battery, so they’ll last longer than wireless ones that eventually die, and it’s a lot harder to lose a wired pair with a long cable than a single earbud.

Now, after more than a decade, Bose has returned to the wired world, but the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are no throwbacks.

One of the few sets of wired earbuds with ANC Comfortable and secure fit High-res audio Simple to use

Call quality isn’t great Wind noise is distracting

The $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect over USB-C, so they don’t need an extra dongle to work with current phones. That’s also how they can offer ANC. Because the 3.5mm or 4.4mm analog audio connector doesn’t provide enough power for active noise cancellation, most wired earbuds, from cheap off-brands to wildly expensive audiophile in-ear monitors , rely on passive isolation only. Bose’s last attempt at wired in-ears with ANC, 2013’s QuietComfort 20 , had a 3.5mm jack, and their ANC relied on a rechargeable battery in the cable. The new Bose earbuds don’t need the battery pack; they can get the minimal power they need for ANC from the USB-C port.

There are a few other USB-C wired headphones with active noise cancellation, but not many. There’s also the $30 Belkin SoundForm ANC Wired Earbuds, which reportedly have weak noise canceling , and Audio-Technica released a pair in Asia earlier this year.

The best part of the Bose earbuds, or any wired earbuds, is that they’re simple. No need to worry about pairing them, no need to charge them, and no need to fiddle with an app. Plug them into the USB-C port on a phone or computer and they just work.

While the noise canceling performance doesn’t measure up to Bose’s Bluetooth earbuds (the wired earbuds have two mics per side, while the QuietComfort Earbuds have three), it’s still solid for the price. It does a great job blocking low-frequency sounds like air conditioners and low truck rumbles, but has difficulty muting conversation (with ANC on, I can’t hear our air conditioner at all, but can make out every word of my wife’s phone conversation as I write this). There’s a slight high-end hiss when the noise canceling is active, but it’s only noticeable when they aren’t playing any sound.

And they sound great. Vocals are clear and bright, and bass is punchy without overwhelming other instruments. I wouldn’t mind being able to cut down the high-end brightness a bit (mainly to tame cymbal ringing), but since these don’t use an app there are no EQ options. The wired connection allows for low latency, so there’s no worry about sound and video lining up, and they support high-res audio at 24-bit/48kHz. I went back and forth between CD quality (16-bit/44.1kHz) and high-res streams of the new release of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul on Qobuz, and the high-res versions sounded a bit more open and spacious. It’s not an enormous difference, but I’d listen to the high-res version on the Bose over the CD-level stream any day.

The in-line remote has three buttons that control volume, playback, and noise-canceling mode selection. They respond quickly when pressed and have a nice rubberized texture. The headphones come with three ear tip sizes and two sets of wings to find a good fit (you don’t even need to use the wings if you find them uncomfortable). I was easily able to find a comfortable combination and they stayed securely in my ears for hours. The earbuds are also IPX4 rated if there’s a light rain while you’re out or you want to use them on a run.

Even with the benefits of wired earbuds, though, nostalgia can’t wipe away the frustrations. If you don’t run the 4.2-foot cable under your shirt, or coil up the excess in your jacket pocket, it catches on everything . In my short time with the Bose, the cable caught on the handle of a kitchen drawer, the edge of my keyboard, the zipper of my sweatshirt, the strap of a bag I was carrying, my pocket (when I accidentally stuffed too much of the excess in with my phone), and even the hand of a stranger who got too close to me in line at Starbucks.

And as with any wired earbuds, there’s cable noise, as vibrations from rubbing or bumping against something travel up the cable to be heard in the earbuds. Although I will say the cable insulation is enough to minimize the effect better than cheap (and older) options.

The Bose struggle with wind. The microphones for noise canceling or transparency mode pick up the wind noise, and it’s distracting — with ANC on, it cuts out the low-end whoosh decently, but the high end is still incredibly present. I found turning it off was best when it was windy outside, although that meant compromising on the noise canceling.

Call quality also isn’t the best. The microphone is on the in-line remote, and it picks up a good amount of ambient sound during calls. If you regularly make calls while walking busy streets, these aren’t the earbuds for you.…

title: EF Cycling Team Parodies Ferrari F1 ‘Unofficial Statement’ Prank in Aftermath of Carapaz Shock Exit
author: Jim Cotton
text:
EF Education-EasyPost parodied the viral “Unofficial Statement” social media post made last week by the Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 team.

At face value, it’s a smart social media tactic to build hype around news of new rider signings.

Below that, the skeptics might say it’s an even smarter PR move to take control of the narrative.

On Friday, marquee rider Richard Carapaz stunned the cycling world and sparked speculation when he broke contract with the team to sign with WorldTour rivals, NSN Cycling.

In its Instagram post on Saturday, EF Education-EasyPost suggested Ben Healy and Sean Quinn “hacked” its social media channels and posted untimely information regarding the 2027 roster. Velo is not aware of any anomalous posts made to the team’s account.

Slide one of the post is an “Unofficial Statement.”

Slide two features Healy and Quinn looking “mischievous.”

The American team’s post is a carbon copy of one made by Scuderia Ferrari at the start of this month.

The Formula 1 powerhouse posted an online “Unofficial Statement” after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc “hijacked” the team’s social media channels. The two superstar drivers had posted a series of bizarre selfies and prank reels to the team’s accounts in the preceding hours.

The Scuderia Ferrari “statement” soon racked up more than two million “likes” and 14,000 comments on Instagram.

“EF Pro Cycling confirms that earlier this week, two individuals within the organization gained unauthorized access to our social media channels.

“During this period, a series of highly questionable editorial decisions were made, including the premature distribution of confidential information regarding our 2027 rider roster. We ask that anyone who received these communications disregard them immediately and refrain from sharing any information until the official announcements begin on October 19.

“We can now confirm that the two suspects have been identified and the situation is now under control.

“We thank our fans for their patience and understanding during this unprecedented incident.”

The Scuderia Ferrari post is at the bottom of this page.

It’s not unusual for teams to build hype for new rider announcements and kit reveals. This prank is well in-line with EF Education-EasyPost’s forward-thinking, unconventional ethos.

We can now expect Jonathan Vaughers’ team to reveal some new signings this coming Monday, October 19.

On Friday, Carapaz broke his ongoing contract for a landmark three-year deal with the budding NSN Cycling Team.

The news blows a huge hole in EF Education-EasyPost.

This year alone, the Ecuadorian finished top-10 at the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, and won two Tour stages. He was by far the squad’s highest-ranked, most recognizable rider.

Carapaz’s exit lit up social media Friday and ignited speculation about EF Education-EasyPost’s future.

The 33-year-old was the seventh rider to confirm they’re leaving the team this winter. Meanwhile, the squad has named only one signing for 2027 – Gavin Sherry, who is promoted from the EF Education-Aevolo devo team.

On Saturday, FE Education-EasyPost attempted to shift the vibes.

title: Bank of England governor walks out of IMF summit in protest against Russia
author: Harry Taylor
text:
Andrew Bailey among finance leaders to leave session in Bangkok when Russian finance minister addressed group

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has taken part in a walkout of finance leaders who left an International Monetary Fund meeting in protest against Russian involvement.

Bailey joined counterparts from France, Germany and a number of Scandinavian and Baltic countries who left the session in Bangkok when the Russian finance minister, Anton Siluanov, addressed the group in Russian.

The Bank of England confirmed that Bailey took part.

The president of the German Bundesbank, Joachim Nagel, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure when Siluanov started speaking.

“The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat told the Reuters news agency.

“We cannot normalise relations with Russia.”

The walkout was acknowledged by the chair of the IMF’s steering committee, the Saudi finance minister, Mohammed al-Jadaan.

Al-Jadaan said: “We came here for a reason, and we achieved ⁠it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters.”

Germany had warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage. Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers this year.

The US has been supportive, with the treasury undersecretary Erin Browne telling Reuters that Washington supported Russia’s presence despite concerns from European countries.

The meeting in the Thai capital heard that the global economy was showing remarkable resilience despite the war between Russia and Ukraine, and in spite of the issues around the strait of Hormuz caused by the US’s bombing campaign.

However, al-Jadaan added that there was no room for complacency, amid public debt levels and high bond market rates.

A statement from al-Jadaan after the IMF meeting said: “The global economy has weathered the latest in a series of shocks better than expected, but buffers have been eroded, and resilience cannot be taken for granted.”

He added: “Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security.”

title: From 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze
author: Alex Daniel
text:
In our second in a series on high-end UK manufacturing, we visit the artisans producing rich clients’ bespoke luxury cars

‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

They are the plaything of kings, presidents and A-listers, with Rolls-Royce enthusiasts ranging from the Sultan of Brunei to Rowan Atkinson, from King Charles III to Kermit the frog .

And at the carmaker’s factory in Goodwood, West Sussex, special requests from customers get more indulgent every year. An interior lined with 3,000 iridescent feathers, or a built-in champagne cooler , or a car built in homage to its owners’ dog, have all become part of the job.

Even with a fast-growing team of artisans and engineers, the company is stretched, and soon it will nearly double the size of its factory as part of a £300m investment by its owner, BMW, which it said at the time of the announcement was part of “securing our future here in the UK”.

Behind much of the demand is a new kind of client, who is younger than ever and with a fortune built in technology, says Julian Jenkins, Rolls-Royce’s director of sales and brand. The average buyer is now just 43 – down from 56 in 2010. “Never has there been so much wealth created so quickly at such a young age,” he says.

Bespoke, high-value customisation is becoming an increasingly valuable pillar of UK manufacturing, which still makes up about 9% of the UK economy despite the years of deindustrialisation that Andy Burnham has vowed to reverse . This week, the wider sector helped drive a surprise expansion of GDP in August, after growing 0.8% month on month.

On a tour of the Goodwood factory, an inner door panel is emblazoned with a bitcoin symbol, hinting at changing tastes. “The industries – cryptocurrency, AI and tech – are where we see some of these young entrepreneurs finding their way very quickly to Rolls-Royce,” Jenkins says. “They are very specific about what they want.”

Another car, built for a wealthy American couple, was devoted to their Labrador, Bailey. The dog’s face was pieced together on a rear panel using more than 180 individual slivers of wood, which was a four-month project, with paw prints engraved in the doors for good measure. Clients nowadays, Jenkins says, “are creating something in their image”.

Four models make up the current Rolls-Royce range: the Phantom, starting at £441,000, the nearly three-tonne Cullinan SUV, from £345,000, the Spectre electric car, from £333,000, and the cheaper Ghost, from £290,000.

But the average Rolls-Royce sells for about £500,000, up from about £300,000 a decade ago, driven largely by customisation work. A heavily personalised car can cost 25% more than the standard price, and seven-figure sums are “not unusual”, a spokesperson says.

“The limits are set by the client,” Jenkins says. “We’ve seen some extremely complex and intricate commissions, and some of those can take multiple years. With that, there is value that comes as a consequence.”

It is a vision Rolls-Royce’s founders could scarcely have imagined for a company that staked its early reputation on reliability. The business dates back to 1904, when Charles Rolls, an aristocrat and racing driver, met Henry Royce, an engineer, at the Midland Hotel in Manchester, and agreed to sell every car the latter could build.

By 1907, Autocar magazine called the Silver Ghost, an early model, the “best car in the world” after completing the gruelling Scottish Reliability Trial without a single mechanical fault. Now, Rolls-Royce has its own entry in the Collins dictionary, as a byword for “anything considered to be the very best of its kind”. Its longest-running model, the Phantom, celebrated its centenary last year.

An expansion into aero engines during the world wars made it a manufacturing powerhouse, but later financial collapse forced the government of the time to nationalise the company in 1971. The car business was split off and sold to the engineering firm Vickers. Rolls-Royce, the FTSE 100 aerospace giant , still shares the same logo.

In 1998, BMW bought the right to put the Rolls-Royce name on cars, and in 2003 opened the Goodwood factory, promising to triple annual production from about 2,000 cars a year. Two decades later it succeeded, when output peaked at 6,032 cars, falling back to 5,664 last year.

Would the Rolls-Royce engineers whose Merlin engines powered the second world war Spitfire have guessed the company name would end up in German hands?

“Rolls-Royce motorcars is very much a British company at heart,” says Chris Brownridge, its chief executive. However, he admits it benefits from “synergies” with BMW, such as “battery technology research and development, access to wind-tunnels and other major facilities”.

The expansion at Goodwood comes as carmakers are under significant strain from Chinese competition, soaring industrial energy costs and US tariffs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs , while Volkswagen, which owns Rolls-Royce’s arch rival Bentley, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030 .

Shrinking demand in China, a key export market for luxury goods, has “obviously been significant”, Jenkins admits, pointing to Rolls-Royce clients “who made their wealth through the [Chinese] property market … which has been adversely affected.”

Electrification has been part of that story, too. Rolls-Royce’s first electric vehicle, the Spectre, launched in 2022, alongside a pledge from the company to sell only EVs by the end of the decade. The model sold briskly at first but deliveries nearly halved in 2025, and earlier this year Rolls-Royce scrapped its 2030 target .

Jenkins says the company is “not immune to the shifts that have happened, and some of the resistance that we’ve seen [to EVs]”. A revamped version, the Spectre Series Two, recently launched with a longer range and more power.…

title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
author: Dominic Preston
text:
Its simplified, hands-free instructions strip out much of what’s essential to online recipes.

Its simplified, hands-free instructions strip out much of what’s essential to online recipes.

When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.

The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious.

There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.”

The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.

The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook.

“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”

It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.

And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous . “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”

Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features . Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.…

title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
text:
United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers

Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?

The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.

The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.

Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.

Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.

Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.

The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.

Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.

There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.

The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen , and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.

UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.

On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.

The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.

The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.

In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.

The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.

Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.

No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
author: Rowena Mason and Dan Milmo
text:
Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors

“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.

It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.

But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.

One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.

Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.

In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.

And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.

A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.

It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”

One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.

Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic , OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.

He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.

But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.

“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.

“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”

The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing , believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.

However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.

“It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.

The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.

Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.…

title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
author: Lesley Evans Ogden, Knowable Magazine
text:
Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect , communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior .

title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
author: Jonathan Watts
text:
Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation

US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.

Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found .

US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.

The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.

In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled ”. The law will come into effect in December.

Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.

It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.

The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.

Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.

Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.

Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.

The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.

Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.

“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”

Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”

US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.

The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”

The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.…

title: Jos Verstappen was hyped like Max - until it all went wrong
author: Matt Beer
text:
The degree to which Jos Verstappen’s own Formula 1 disappointment fuelled everything he poured into son Max’s preparation for his ultimately-phenomenal F1 career is already part of motorsport folklore.

The element that perhaps gets overlooked now is how good Jos’s own F1 career was supposed to be - that there was a period, a short one admittedly, when there was just as much excitement over Jos’s prospects as a future F1 champion as there was over Max’s arrival on the F1 grid in 2015.

As the latest episode of our new F1 Rewind podcast series with Edd Straw and Mark Hughes explores, it’s a test for Footwork at Estoril in late September 1993 that really starts the hype.

Only two years out of karting, and having just won the German Formula 3 title, 21-year-old Jos sets a time that would’ve put his very middling car 10th on the grid for the previous weekend’s Portuguese Grand Prix. Track evolution played a part in his time, but the impression his overall performance makes is huge. Verstappen gets the cover slot on the next week’s Autosport magazine, which declares him ‘F1’s hottest new boy’.

Edd Straw: “If you look at Jos Verstappen's career record and didn't experience it or live through it, it's really easy to underestimate how big an impact this test really made."

Mark Hughes: “He was a seriously hot property at that time. He came straight in from karting and won championship immediately in GM Lotus in the Benelux Championship. He'd done a one-off guest appearance in the bigger league GM Lotus series at Spa. He was sensational in that.

“He moved straight to Formula 3, won the German championship, dominated it, and looked set to set the F1 tracks alight.

“The teams were falling over themselves trying to get him on a long-term contract. If you were looking for where the next Michael Schumacher or Mika Hakkinen might be, that's where you are looking. No question.”

Edd Straw: “Everybody was talking to him basically. McLaren gave him a test at one stage. Obviously Benetton, who he eventually signed for. There was a little bit of Ferrari interest even. It was an absolute clamour because this was the next mega-star.

“Also because of how rapid his ascent was. Karting to F1 in two years. In recent years we’ve got a bit more used to really fast ascents, such as Max Verstappen’s. But that was really, really rare at this point.

“So you've not only got this driver who is considered to be incredible, but he's on this rocketship to F1 as well.

“And if in late 1993 you were saying, ‘right, who is going to come into F1 and win races and be a future world champion?’ Jos Verstappen is the name people would have picked out.”

Mark Hughes: “Overwhelmingly at that time. There was no question. He was on the verge of something big.”

Verstappen and manager Huub Rothengatter pick Benetton, which is offering a season of testing and preparation in 1994 then a guaranteed race seat - either in its own squad, or placed elsewhere - for 1995.

But rather than getting a year of learning outside the spotlight, Verstappen is thrust into Benetton’s second race seat alongside Michael Schumacher when JJ Lehto is injured in a testing crash.

Verstappen ultimately gets two stints in that seat, with Lehto still struggling on his return and having to step away again, before being benched at the end of the season so Benetton can evaluate Johnny Herbert in that car.

It adds up to 10 of the 16 1994 rounds in the second Benetton, with Verstappen earning two podiums, but also being sent into a terrifying aerial crash on his debut in Brazil in a pile-up triggered by Eddie Irvine and being caught up in the infamous German GP pit fire.

Later admitting he found the Schumacher-centric car “too nervous” for him, Verstappen never outqualified or even once led Schumacher at the end of a racing lap in their eight outings together with a massive 1.920s (2.288%) average deficit.

Going up against Schumacher in the same team as an underprepared rookie, amid a season of turmoil, was a tall order. And it was enough to instantly crush all that career momentum and hype Verstappen had carried into F1.

Mark Hughes: “In hindsight, he wasn't ready, he came in too early. Had the original plan played out, he would have been getting a lot of mileage away from the spotlight of grands prix and would have probably come in much better prepared in 1995.

“Not only that, Benetton was absolutely centred around Michael Schumacher and team boss Flavio Briatore was into driver management and then making money on drivers.

“Rothengatter and Verstappen had unknowingly surrendered control of his own destiny. As well as being in essentially just the second string car in a team that was totally focused around one driver, Verstappen wasn't even going to be in charge of where he was going to go next.”

Edd Straw: “He has this weird season and actually a big chunk of that career momentum's wiped out by that first season. It really, really is. It's not gone. There's still a residual, ‘oh this guy's good’, but already pretty much the die is cast.”

Mark Hughes: “It saps you of energy when you get into a situation like that where you're the second driver and you're not the focus of anything. And you've been used to being at the absolute centre of everything. You've been used to being treated as a megastar in the making and with everything centred around you in the junior category, with everybody there for you, everybody on your side. And suddenly to be in the lackey role, I think it does damage you.

“And not only that, but you're going up against Michael Schumacher as a rookie.

“And in his more reflective later years, Verstappen also said that even disregarding the equipment differences - and there were significant equipment differences at Benetton - and even disregarding all the factors against him, when you looked at some of the things that Michael was able to do close up and suddenly have to say to yourself, ‘I came in thinking I was going to win races, I think I'm going to win the championship, I'm going to beat everybody’ and then you come up against somebody like that and you think, ‘no, maybe I have to recalibrate here’.

“And even Verstappen acknowledges that maybe he wasn't Michael Schumacher.

“But he was pretty good. Better than he was able to show subsequently.”

Watch or listen to F1 Rewind for much more on Jos’s F1 career, including the later big opportunities that fell through, and an in-depth look at how it all fed into the way he handled Max’s upbringing and journey towards F1.

title: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
author: Heather Stewart in Bangkok and Graeme Wearden
text:
Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last

I nside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.

A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.

“Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared.

Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development.

Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO).

According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP.

It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict.

The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies.

Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks.

The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic.

That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time.

“Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said.

Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth.

The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.”

Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another.

The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year.

The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates.

The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence.

“The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.

“Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.”

Unusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period.

The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism.

The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.”…
