title: Searching for a future – The riders still without a contract for 2027
author: Matilda Price
text:
The transfer market has been in full swing since August, with dozens of riders changing teams all across the peloton, and dozens more extending with their current teams. Many of these deals are done as early as the spring, with other decisions continuing to be made through the summer.

But as the off-season, the winter and the new year rapidly approach, October marks the time when those riders who don’t yet have a contract for next year start to worry.

Deals can be struck late on, yes, but rosters are starting to fill up, and with a few big names still on the market, a lot of teams want to leave themselves some flexibility until the last minute.

For riders, though, that means they can be left scrambling and having to rethink their futures.

At the time of writing, over 120 WorldTour riders don’t have an officially announced contract for 2027, with hundreds more still contractless at the ProTeam level. Some of those may know where they’re going to be racing; it just hasn’t been announced yet, whilst some are still weighing up their options and making a decision, and some are desperately trying to find a spot for 2027.

With rosters rapidly filling up, here are some significant names who are still without an official contract for 2027.

Various outlets and journalists have linked him with several different teams, including Lotto-Intermarché and Tudor, and there are multiple teams in the peloton that would surely be interested in signing the multiple-time Grand Tour winner and current European TT champion. But so far, the 36-year-old hasn’t been officially tied down to any team, and we don’t know where, if anywhere, his signature will land for 2027.

Roglič is in a better position than most, because it seems like he definitely has options on the table – he can certainly continue racing if he wants to – but that doesn’t mean that it’s an easy decision to make. A lot of other deals might be hanging on the outcome of Roglič’s transfer, too, so this is a significant contract to follow at this late point in the window.

Former Giro d’Italia winner Tao Geoghegan Hart has never quite been the same since his crash and severe injuries sustained at the Giro in 2023, and though Lidl-Trek put their faith in him with a three-year contract, he hasn’t been able to rediscover his Grand Tour-winning level since then. Now, six years after he took home the maglia rosa, it’s not clear whether we’ll see him in the peloton at all next year.

Earlier in the year, the prevailing talk around the paddock was that Geoghegan Hart was set for a quiet retirement, but more recently, Daniel Benson has reported that a move to EF Education-EasyPost could be on the cards.

Nothing has been confirmed yet, though, and if a deal hasn’t already been signed, his run of DNFs in the last months won’t have helped in getting something across the line. Geoghegan Hart was once one of the best riders of his generation, but will now likely take a pay cut at the very least, if he does want to continue in the peloton.

Lucinda Brand recently confirmed her exit from Lidl-Trek , opting to stay with Baloise Verzekeringen–Het Poetsbureau Lions cyclo-cross but giving an answer about her future on the road. In an Instagram post at the time, she suggested there was news coming on that subject, so it seems likely that she does indeed have a road contract for 2027, but it’s yet to be announced.

An extremely experience and successful racer who is clearly still firing on all cylinders, it seems unlikely that Brand would struggle to find a spot for 2027, but the fact that nothing has been announced yet could point to her looking wider than the WorldTour for her future.

After nine seasons in the WorldTour, James Knox may be facing the end of the road this season as he has struggled to find a new team, with no extension forthcoming at Picnic PostNL after the expiry of his one-year contract.

"Of course I wish I did have something," he told at Il Lombardia. "I would still cross my fingers, but the reality of the situation with cycling now, with limited space for the WorldTour teams, many, many quality riders, a lot of focus on points, and younger riders coming through with guaranteed contracts from development teams… I think it's become a situation where it might be hard for me to get anything for next year. I don’t know what will come of it."

Though not a prolific winner himself, Knox has established himself as a dependable climbing domestique, but that's perhaps one of most competitive areas on the transfer market, and as a result, it might be a premature end to his road career this winter.

Gaia Realini agreed to depart Lidl-Trek this year despite having a year left on her contract, and whilst she reportedly has interest from other teams, nothing is confirmed yet, and we're still waiting to hear the exact details of her future.

Often, if riders are leaving teams early, it's because they have a better offer somewhere else already, but it's not always as clear-cut as that. Sometimes things simply aren't working out, or the team want to free up space to bring in another rider by striking a deal with an existing one to leave early, so such an exit doesn't always mean that something else is already lined up.

A talented climber with plenty of potential, Realini seems primed to find a new home, but we'll wait to see where.

Belgian veteran Tom Van Asbroeck is a mainstay of the professional peloton, and the winner of Classics like Binche-Chimay-Binche as well as a respected Classics road captain, but at 36 he’s joining the legion of older riders who would like to continue their careers, but struggle to find a spot to do so.

Van Asbroeck told that he was expecting his contract to be renewed for 2027, but things changed when NSN received "an opportunity the team couldn't pass up" and his future with the team came at the expense of a new signing.

"I hope for the team's sake that they have made the right decision, but it leaves me with a bitter feeling," he said. "It is strange that I was deemed good enough for a Tour selection and numerous major races, but now there is suddenly no place for me anymore. That is contradictory and particularly confronting."

At the other end of the spectrum from Van Asbroeck, there are riders who are only just starting their careers but find themselves faced with an early hurdle of not having a team. This seems to be the situation facing France's Alexy Faure Prost , who joined Picnic PostNL this year but is facing retirement at only 22.

"There's only one step between being among the world's best in your category, being courted by the biggest teams, and being forgotten while being even stronger than before," his girlfriend wrote in an Instagram post that Faure Prost collaborated with.

"Finding another contract back or simply renewing for another year on the same team is becoming more and more impossible. No, ending a professional career at 22 is not normal. Behind all the training data and contract money, there is always a human, not a robot."

Will professional sport understand one day that taking young people from junior ranks to the highest level is also about accompanying them? Not just putting them in races. I sincerely hope that a team gets this message and that it's way too early for you to stop showing your talent."

Neo-pros must be given a minimum of two years on their first contract, but after that, many face uncertain futures and the harsh reality of the world of future talent, where if you don't prove yourself at a young age, you might not be able to continue at all.

As the chances of finding a contract get narrower and narrower, many riders have started to come to terms with the fact that this may be the end of the road for them, and have started sharing their stories on social media. Asbjørn Hellemose did that over the weekend, confirming he won't be continuing with Jayco AlUla next year.

"With how the transfer market looks at the moment, I will most likely not continue as a WorldTour rider at all," the 27-year-old Dane wrote on Instagram after Lombardia.

"At the moment, I’m not sure what’s next for me. When the season is over, I will have time to sit down calmly and reflect on what the best next step for me will be. What I do know is that I’m extremely proud of what I have achieved with my talent and a lot of hard work. Four years in the WorldTour, with participation in one Grand Tour, one World Championships and four Monuments as some of the highlights. Who would have thought that when I was still a teenager living in Denmark?"

Hellemose's situation is far from unique, and is a sad one where riders don't get the heartfelt send-off that other retiring (by choice) riders did at races like Il Lombardia and Paris-Tours, but are forced out of the professional peloton when they feel they still have more to give.

With well over 100 WorldTour riders still not officially confirmed on teams for 2027, and plenty of squads still with roster spots open for next year, the transfer market is still very much alive, even if it feels like we've seen lots of moves already. title: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes
author: David Smith in Washington
text:
The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy

D avid Agus’s first encounter with Elizabeth Holmes at a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.

“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” Agus, a medical oncologist , recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”

Holmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founder Steve Jobs .

Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of state Henry Kissinger and George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment.

Margaret O’Mara , a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered .”

Perhaps the answer lies in You Can See Everything , a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy.

That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and established Theranos , promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood.

She found a receptive audience among investors who wanted Silicon Valley to deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains: “ She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech.

“The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’”

O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.”

Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m. Theranos had published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms.

Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of the Ellison Medical Institute , comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability.

“I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.”

By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists.

The New Yorker wrote : “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.”

The heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during the Ronald Reagan era. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s. O’Mara says: “He was drawn in by the idea that here is a bright young person trying to do something more meaningful than building an app. But there wasn’t enough due diligence.”

In his biography, In the Nation’s Service , journalist Philip Taubman describes how people around Shultz worried that his enthusiasm had become entangled with personal affection for Holmes. Shultz spoke to her by phone almost daily and invited her to family Christmas dinners. Holmes encouraged his attention, leaning in close when they sat together.

Shultz even encouraged his grandson, Tyler Shultz , to take a summer internship at Theranos before joining the company full-time. Tyler eventually became convinced that Holmes was exaggerating what her technology could do. He took his concerns to the Wall Street Journal, whose investigation into the company was crucial to unravelling its web of deceit.…

title: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold
author: Jeffrey Ingold
text:
If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …

D o you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.

I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system.

If you went to see a play and the ticket said the show started at 7.30pm, you’d rightly be annoyed if after 20 minutes the performance still hadn’t started. Yet when it comes to watching movies, we’ve collectively accepted that it’s fine for them to start later than advertised. Which also means we all put up with people coming in late, shining their phone torches and bumping into you because they tried to show up when the film actually starts.

Now that almost a third of wide releases run over two hours and pre-show advertising and trailers last for 20-30 minutes, something’s gotta give. I say films should start on time. I know a better moviegoing experience is possible. I grew up in Canada, where our cinemas played their films at the ticketed time and the ads started earlier. When my family showed up 10 minutes late to The Fellowship of the Ring, we missed the entire opening sequence explaining the history of the rings of power. We deserved that!

A brave senator in Connecticut tried to tackle this injustice in 2025 with a bill that would “ require the disclosure of accurate movie start times in advertisements and listings ”. However, it was watered down to a mere “working group” after pushback from cinema operators. They warned they’d lose vital revenue if advertisers pulled back because people started skipping the pre-show entirely. Erin Brockovich wouldn’t have given in so easily.

How can we succeed where the Connecticut senator failed? Simple: we also get rid of assigned seating. Say goodbye to paying £26 for an Ultra Lux recliner if you want the best view. It’s a flat fee no matter where you sit. Welcome to the Hunger Games of cinema seating.

If you want a “good” seat for a film, you have to earn it by showing up early. Exactly like when I was young, the ads and trailers will play before the start time so the film can begin promptly. Arrive on time, after the trailers, and you might be stuck in the front row, but that’s on you for avoiding the ads.

I’m just a cinephile, standing in front of a movie theatre, asking it to respect me and my time. Why is that so hard?

Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and culture

title: Squash down: smaller pumpkins expected this Halloween after drought in England
author: Helena Horton
text:
Data shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carving

In the lead-up to Halloween , front porches across the country feature fat, proudly carved pumpkins, lit from within by tea lights.

But this year there is likely to be a shortage due to drought, experts have warned, with the squashes much smaller than usual.

Mini pumpkins will have to be used, and some have suggested that those celebrating the spooky festival draw faces on vegetables instead of carving them.

England has faced a punishing drought for most of this year, which has dramatically affected harvests. Data has found that this year could be the worst harvest on record as farmers struggled to irrigate their crops.

Pumpkins are 90% water, and need a lot of it to grow. The vegetables are native to the Americas and were brought over in the Tudor period, during the 16th century.

Guy Singh-Watson, the founder of organic veg box company Riverford, said: “After such an extraordinarily hot, dry summer, it’s not surprising that Halloween pumpkins are smaller than usual as they are mostly water. But perhaps it’s time we questioned our obsession with giant carving pumpkins in the first place.”

Shunning pumpkins would go some way to bringing the carving of vegetables tradition back to its roots. The custom began in 17th-century Britain while marking the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which was when spirits were thought to roam the Earth.

Rather than pumpkins, root vegetables such as celeriac, turnips and mangelwurzels were carved into grotesque faces, and some believed they could ward off evil spirits.

Guy Barter, the chief horticulturalist at the Royal Horticultural Society, said: “Pumpkins are on the small side this year unless heavily watered. Such drought makes watering sufficiently very difficult to accomplish in practice. Pumpkins are relatively drought-tolerant but this year the weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.

“The heat later and some drought stress caused fruits to ripen earlier than usual. Their dry matter content and rind hardness are both excellent so the crop should store well, although commercial pumpkins become worthless the day after Halloween. That’s a pity as they make lovely soups until the new year when the much tastier winter squashes take over.”

Singh-Watson said the growing of a large, watery squash simply to throw it away after Halloween was wasteful, adding: “I’ve enjoyed growing pumpkins before, they’re a lovely crop, but the idea of growing something that’s going to be thrown away has become increasingly difficult to justify. Growing any crop comes with an environmental cost, and generating a mountain of waste without feeding anyone makes little sense.”

The vegetable entrepreneur has been growing a selection of small, colourful squashes and is now selling a box containing a selection including crown prince, red onion, sweet lightning, futsu and stripetti. He said: “This time of the year should be a celebration of the wonderful abundance of seasonal vegetables that see us through autumn and winter. Squash come in an extraordinary variety of shapes, sizes and colours, and offer just as much decorative potential, with considerably more flavour. Let’s paint a face on a squash instead … and then eat it.”

Some gardeners have been trying novel methods to try to get the size of pumpkins up.

Ali Goding, the garden manager at RHS Harlow Carr in North Yorkshire, said: “Pumpkins struggle to grow in heavy clay soil during drought conditions, so the team at RHS garden Harlow Carr have trialled a new, novel way to grow pumpkins this year – in a compost cake which helps retain moisture, humidity and warmth and the results have been fantastic while also benefiting wildlife.

“They have set with hard skins in the heat so should store well and they will also have a good flavour with all that sun.

“Normally we are a bit cool, damp and too far north for them to develop a full flavour – so the extra heat worked out well for us. A good year!”

title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
author: Matthew Weaver
text:
Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem

T he leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders.

A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain.

The stink is so acrid that the Bicycle Nation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside.

The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit.

Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem.

Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak.

The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”.

When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air.

“It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.”

He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.”

The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system , just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era.

Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out.

Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.”

The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced.

Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts , in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion.

Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.”

When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.”

Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.”

Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicycle Nation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive.

Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.”

And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.”

Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.”

Polocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.”

The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz.

A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”

title: Yankees news: The second base conundrum
author: Jake Devin
text:
The unsettled second base situation; ex-Yankee Bauers is NLCS MVP; the future of Stanton.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The Athletic | Chris Kirschner : The Yankees are reportedly unlikely to give Jazz Chisholm Jr. a qualifying offer, and it seems like the second baseman’s time in the Bronx is just about over. That leaves the question: what do the Yankees do at second base? Captain Aaron Judge seems to have his preferred choice, telling reporters after the Yankees’ ALDS exit, “If we were gonna go win the World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team.” Volpe did look comfortable at second after losing his shortstop job to George Lombard Jr., but Volpe’s work with the bat still leaves plenty to be desired. Luis García Jr. is an interesting option; he’s played second before (albeit with terrible defensive metrics), and looked so skilled defensively at first this year that he could convince you his agility and arm strength would play elsewhere on the diamond.

New York Daily News | Peter Sblendorio : There haven’t been many ex-Yankees kicking around postseason, but one former Bomber has figured prominently in Jake Bauers. Bauers played for the club in 2023 and got off to a hot start, hitting a home run in his first game and posting a .899 OPS over his first ten games with the Yankees.

Bauers couldn’t keep it going that year (neither could the Yankees) and New York ended up trading him in the offseason to the Brewers in exchange for minor league outfielder Jace Avina, who is now the Yankees’ No. 24 rated prospect by MLB Pipeline. On the other end, Bauers has blossomed with the Brewers, running an .874 OPS this season and taking home deserved 2026 NLCS MVP honors.

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch : Hoch delivers his offseason preview for the Yankees, running down some of the big questions. Among them is the aforementioned second base situation, as well as the matter of what to do with Giancarlo Stanton, Austin Wells’ future with the Yankees, and David Bednar’s fate. Unlike Chisholm, Bednar appears likely to receive a qualifying offer, which is slated to come in at about $23 million for the 2027 season.

The Athletic | Tim Britton : The upcoming MLB free agent class is among the worst in recent memory, and The Athletic looked at the last decade of free agent classes with the benefit of hindsight to get a sense of where this group may fall. The lowest-ranked class ends up as 2017, when the top hitters to sign were Yoenis Cespedes, Dexter Fowler, and Ian Desmond, while the top pitchers were Aroldis Chapman, Kenley Jansen, and Rich Hill. The saving grace for the current crop of free agents is a fairly deep group of pitching targets, headlined by Tarik Skubal but backed up by Michael King, Sonny Gray, Kevin Gausman, and Freddy Peralta. That’s somewhat unfortunate news for the Yankees, who nary need an arm but have an offense that could use reinforcements.

title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin wins again on stage 5 as Paul Magnier crashes in final kilometre
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Milan Fretin (Cofidis) struck again at the Tour of Guangxi, the Belgian prevailing in a bunch sprint in Yizhou as overall leader Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) crashed in the final kilometre.

As was the case in the previous four stages of the race, stage 5 was always set to come down to a mass sprint finish, and so it proved as the peloton once again raced to finish as one.

The sprint was set up after the break of the day – featuring Patrick Gamper, Jasha Sütterlin (JaycoAlUla), Brandon Rivera (Netcompany Ineos), Baptiste Veistroffer (Lotto-Intermarché), Davide Formolo (Movistar), and Max Walker (EF Education-EasyPost) was caught 14km from the finish.

Magnier, the winner of stages 1 and 4, looked to be the favourite once again, but the Frenchman didn't make the sprint, crashing along with Max Kanter (XDS-Astana) and several others as the peloton raced towards the finish line.

A host of other top sprinters at the race avoided the carnage to contest victory, and it was Arvid de Kleijn (Tudor) who launched the dash for the line. Instead, it was Fretin who came out on top, timing his run just right to beat Matteo Moschetti (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Erlend Blikra (Uno-X Mobility) to the win.

Magnier may not have added to his win tally, but he can rest assured that he'll continue in the race lead after the stage, heading into stage 6 with a 10-second lead over stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL), who was also held up in the crash.

He's unlikely to hold the jersey all the way to the finish on Sunday, however, with the closing stage heading for the race's only uphill finish at Nongla Scenic Spot (3.2km at 7.3%).

title: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
text: History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation. title: What one image can't show you about Rwanda F1 track
author: Jon Noble
text:
If you adapted the saying 'you should never judge a book by its cover' for the world of Formula 1, then tracks should never be deemed successes or failures based solely on rendered images of them.

What can look like nice lines on a bit of paper are no guarantee that a circuit will be good for racing.

Equally, corners that are spectacular and a thrill for drivers - such as Eau Rouge at Spa, the Degners at Suzuka, or even La Monumental at the newer Madring - look simple affairs when just viewed on a screen.

The disparity between the impression a track render can give and what the reality of a track is like when built is a topic that has come up in recent days following the reveal of the layout of the new F1 track in Rwanda.

The single image released of the new Rise Motordrome track near Kigali, which will host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s, drew mixed responses from fans - which was perhaps fuelled by some of the key elements of the layout not being visible.

That inevitably prompted debate about whether the track was going to be any good for overtaking.

After years working on the project, and thousands of laps of it on a simulator, track designer Alex Wurz is enthusiastic about what has been pulled together.

And there are so many details to the circuit, which will feature the greatest elevation change over a lap of the season, that are not possible to pick out from the render, according to Wurz.

"To give you a little flavour, in Turn 2, we are coming downhill with top speed," he tells The Race. "It's 10.8% [gradient] exactly. We're going into a very high compression with 12% banking, and then going 14% uphill, so you will only see sky.

"Towards the end of the corner from the 12% banking we are going to 6%, and then 4%. And in the sim, this feels just like pure joy.

"My favourite section is coming out of the canopy corner over the crest into the lake.

"The timing of it is that you just get light [as the car rises over the crest] and then suddenly you get a 10% compression, and from there you know your mind has to engage into the fast Esses.

"Those are the corners I think should resonate with the fans in the simulator, on your computer games, but hopefully with the big dogs - the F1 drivers themselves."

An emphasis on 'fighting'

As a former F1 driver and Le Mans 24 Hours winner, Wurz knows an awful lot about what makes a top-line track, and what ingredients are needed to help make a good race.

He says it is naive to think that overtaking can ever be guaranteed by a track layout because passing is influenced so much by car regulations, details on the day such as tyre degradation levels, and even whether a frontrunner has made a mess of qualifying.

What he thinks is critical though is to produce a track that allows drivers to "fight" each other, and that can only come from how corners are sequenced.

"We have wide open corners with corner sequences 1/2/3, where it means attack, defend, attack, defend," he says. "Now if I defended too much, I might be overtaken, or I'm so slow that the next guy is catching up. So, it is initiating fighting.

"If it finally is the track where the most overtakes are going to happen, to be honest, that's random. It depends which tyre manufacturer, and what tyre degradation on that day will happen.

"But it's a drivers' and riders' circuit. It's made for overtaking and fighting, and I think it should tick all those boxes."

Wurz has faith that what he has designed will not just be good for fighting, but also be a challenge that drivers enjoy.

"I think it will be an amazing circuit for racing, but equally for the drivers," he said. "If people like comparisons, I don't like them too much, but with red wine, you speak about berries and oak flavours.

"So, if we do the same with tracks, you could compare some of the sections to Spa because of the ups and downs and the speed and the flow. Of course, also Suzuka is one of every driver's favourites, and there's some flavours which you could compare.

"But it's all authentic and bespoke to the topography; it's flowing, it's fast, but we do have, of course, heavy braking areas."

One important element that is shared by a lot of tracks is elevation change, something that pretty much all top-ranking venues have.

The 197 metres of elevation that the Rwanda layout boasts should deliver something that will make even the straights spectacular, and was not obvious from the render - which The Race has subsequently produced more of.

The back straight for example, which was actually hidden from the images, plunges downhill before a proper compression as it rises up again into a heavy braking area.

There are also complex braking areas that are being built. "On the render, you don't see the long straight well, and you don't see the hairpins," says Wurz.

Effort has gone into creating tight turns with combined braking/turning where drivers are exposed to greater risks of getting things wrong - and therefore being attacked from behind.

"What is really challenging is if you are combining forces: your braking, your turning, to then optimise all four contact patches at the right slip angle," says Wurz.

"So those corners where you arrive at 300km/h and you break down to something like 80km/h or 100km/h, but with long combined phases, they are the ones where you can do the real divebombs. And we have three of those.

"I think those will be the sneaky overtakes. And if you start to defend, again, then your next straight line will be three and a half to four tenths down. And that triggers the fighting.

"And if there is no overtaking from that, triggering the fighting means someone else is coming. So I think it should at least initiate great fighting."

Wurz has consulted a lot of driver friends with ideas for the layout, and says that feedback has been positive.

While he has not identified those he has consulted, he says that drivers with a total of 12 FIA world championships have been involved. As chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, the likelihood is that some of those titles were from F1.

Wurz thinks that, in order to make a layout a good drivers' circuit, it is critical that drivers have input on what works.

"I am in almost everyday contact with the greatest champions of current times, so I do show them tracks," he says. "I do listen to what is said about corner sections and which are rewarding and not rewarding.

"They always have some tips, but the principle layout was seen by one guy who texted me back he said: 'That will be instantly one of the most classic favourite circuits of all drivers.' And I really hope so because it is a lot of work!"

And if you want a hint of the way that the track layout has been shaped by thinking about the challenge drivers face, then there is no better example than the Esses section at the end of the lap.

Wurz says this area, which looks similar to but is not a carbon copy of the Suzuka Esses, is one that is going to punish greedy drivers who try to attack it too much.

"If you get one element wrong, the next five or six corners are off," he says. "That's havoc in your brain, but it's joy if you manage it.

"You are coming around the lake out of the forest corner, which is a really cool corner because it's only forest and the track, and then you come over a hill into a double right-hander.

"Here the lift in the stomach should be perfectly timed to then get the compression on the apex. And from this moment on, every movement you do on your instruments are important: steering, throttle and brake.

"None of the corners are flat. Everything has to be either just a downshift or dab on the brake. You really need to flow from one to the next.

"If you do a little mistake, it's designed that greed is penalising you. And this is so cool for the drivers because you kind of have to hold back a little bit, but you want to exceed it.

"If you slide half a metre too wide, that means you have already 0.15 seconds gone, so you have to be true to yourself. And this is a type of mind game.

"Suzuka does it very well. That's why all the drivers love it, and hopefully we can be in the same category of racetrack as the great ones."

title: Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
text:
Exclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisis

Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.

The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.

Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work.

With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people.

The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time.

After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships .

Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade.

Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access.

Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.

“Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.”

Earlier this year Labour revamped the apprenticeship levy introduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses.

Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs.

Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027.

Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme has enrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months , against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament.

This month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships.

However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered over employer national insurance contributions and as firms press for budget support to help them hire more young people.

Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse.

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed.

“We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice.

“The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

title: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
author: Aseel Mousa
text:
Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry

Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.

Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.

“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”

Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.

Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.

On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.

“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”

Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”

Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.

Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.

In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”

Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.

“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”

Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.

“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”

Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.

Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.

When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.

The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.

Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.

As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.

By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”

In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.…

title: Call for more food funding due to high living cost
text:
A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools.

Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme.

Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families".

The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment.

The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools.

Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead.

The topic was debated 29 September , external in the States Assembly.

Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that".

But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme.

"Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said.

When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option".

She added she understood people's concerns around the freshness of the food but her "understanding is that the meals are actually frozen rather than artificially preserved".

"I would like to see these funded meals extended further because it hits the cost of living for parents and... provides healthy meals for children," she said.

title: Charity reflects on changing needs over 25 years
text:
A charity that raises funds to provide children with "essential items" has said families are facing "changing pressures" as celebrates its 25th anniversary.

Help a Guernsey Child said since it was created in 2001 it has provided more than £1.2m worth of essential items, equipment, services and support to local children and young people.

The charity said in its early years it gave financial support to a number of larger community projects benefiting children but there was now an increasing focus on helping individual children and families.

Alex Jenner, from Help a Guernsey Child, said: "Over the past 25 years, we have seen significant changes in the types of support families require."

Jenner said despite changes in needs the charity's "purpose has remained the same, to ensure that children in the Bailiwick are not disadvantaged because they lack the essentials that every child deserves".

The charity said it works through professional referrers who know the children and families involved.

Applications for grants come in from social workers, health visitors, teachers, doctors, nurses and other frontline professionals and are considered individually by the charity's Directors.

The charity said the increasing focus on helping in individual cases meant providing something as "fundamental as a bed, flooring, white goods, clothing, safety equipment or a heating appliance, as well as specialist disability equipment and educational opportunities".

It added the nature of their work reflected the "changing pressures" faced by local families.

These included the rising cost of living and increased demand for essential household items and practical support, it said.

Jenner said: "A relatively small grant at exactly the right time can make a profound difference to a child's safety, wellbeing, education or independence."

title: Nightclubs are disappearing - and it's affecting young people
text:
Under-30s have described missing out on being able to "let loose and mess around" because of a "bleak" lack of nightlife where they live.

Henry Gannon said that growing up in Woking he had seen places for young people to gather and socialise "die away".

"Communal areas just seem to have vanished," he added.

Woking once had multiple late-night venues - now it does not have any traditional dedicated nightclubs left in the town centre.

Gannon blamed the situation on the cost of living crisis, which he said was "pricing out" those in their 20s from enjoying themselves.

"There isn't really anything to do for younger people who often don't have much expendable income," he said.

Alternative options, the 23-year-old added, were "Wetherspoons, sitting in the park or getting a prohibitively expensive taxi back from another town or city".

"I feel like I am missing out on a crucial part of being my age, which is being able to let loose, mess around and enjoy life.

A quarter of UK towns have lost all their nightclubs, the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) said in 2025.

It added that one in six towns have no late-night venues left.

"These figures are a stark warning of the systematic erosion of Britain's nightlife infrastructure," said NTIA CEO Michael Kill.

"We are facing a national cultural crisis.

"The damage, as we see it, is increasingly irreversible. Once these venues disappear, they rarely return."

Adam said the nightlife situation in Tonbridge - where the last club closed several years ago - was "pretty minimal".

"There are some nice pubs and small bars, though most things close around midnight," he said.

But the 29-year-old, originally from the US, said he was drawn to Kent town as it was "quieter and more relaxed".

Still, Adam said, the lack of nightlife forced younger people to go elsewhere for a night out, which impacted the local economy.

"It is definitely a missed opportunity," he added.

While he recognised nightclubs were spaces for meeting others, Adam said there was also a trend of younger people going out and drinking less - which was good for their health.

The twenty-somethings going out - in the gym

The BBC previously heard from under-30s that were opting out of drinking culture and getting their "social fix" from the gym .

They said that alcohol-free socialising was empowering, avoided hangovers and let them meet like-minded people.

Others have also pointed to a cultural shift with more people skipping clubs for sober social events .

Finn Ashcroft, from Chichester in West Sussex, said after Covid "people were finding it harder to get out and socialise".

However, he said it was important to emphasise that many under-30s were "making do" without clubs and instead creating their own events.

While its traditional nightclubs had closed, Ashcroft said Chichester had plenty of spaces that could be used for music and dancing.

He told the BBC he had set up the event companies C-Side Sounds and Strictly Grooves to "push music locally" in these spaces.

"Students were champing at the bit for somewhere to go," he said.

"We've definitely helped nurture nightlife within the city."

The 22-year-old said the "most important thing" people looking for more nightlife where they live could do was "be vocal about it".

"They have the power to [get] local councils and governing bodies to make sure there are spaces for people... to make memories together."

title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
text:
Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use

NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.

Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.

The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in the NHS of a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”

According to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”

Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.

Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson, saying last week : “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.

Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.

But two parliamentary select committees have urged the government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.

“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”

Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.

“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.

Palantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.

“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministers stating that it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”

It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.

Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHS England has, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.

The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this week urged ministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.…

title: UK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pension
author: Rupert Jones
text:
Fixed-term annuities give income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end

Financial firms are reporting growing demand for a product that helps bridge the gap between stopping work and getting your pension.

Sales of retirement annuities have risen sharply during the last couple of years, and now advisers are seeing a fresh surge of interest in what they say is one of the market’s “lesser-known” options.

An annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income. The vast majority of people opt for one that provides an income for the rest of their life, called a lifetime annuity.

But more individuals are now buying a version that gives them an income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end. They can then decide what to do with that cash based on their circumstances at the time.

This type of product is called a fixed-term annuity, and the retirement specialist Standard Life says it can be a way to secure a guaranteed income for a set period while giving you the flexibility to review your options later.

After falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular partly because of higher annuity rates and tax changes, but also because they offer some financial certainty during turbulent times.

On top of that, a fixed-term annuity can give some breathing space if, say, you don’t feel quite ready to sign up to a lifetime annuity or go into drawdown (where you withdraw a portion of your pension savings every year and leave the rest invested).

Standard Life says its data reveals there has been growing customer interest in fixed-term annuities this year, while its rival Canada Life said recently it had experienced a “significant rise in demand” for its version of this product.

So how much income might you get from a fixed-term annuity?

This week Standard Life said a 62-year-old with a £100,000 pension pot could currently get a guaranteed income of about £13,800 a year for five years, and would get a £50,000 lump sum at the end of the term.

This level of income is higher than the full new state pension of £12,548 a year. You get that when you reach state pension age, which has started to rise from 66 and will hit 67 in April 2028.

According to the latest Standard Life research, 62 is, on average, the age when people would like to retire. So someone could use a fixed-term annuity to fund the period between stopping work and getting their state pension, providing some financial certainty.

Nick Flynn at Canada Life says these types of products are resonating with retirees “because they solve real challenges, helping retirees buy time before committing to drawdown or purchasing a lifetime annuity”.

He adds: “Customers are choosing the product to bridge the gap to state pension or defined benefit pension start dates, help fund specific commitments such as mortgage payments or school fees, or stabilise income in the earlier years of retirement.”

Changes to the inheritance tax (IHT) treatment of pensions , announced by Rachel Reeves in the 2024 autumn budget, have helped give annuities a new lease of life.

The then chancellor announced that from April 2027, money left in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after someone’s death will no longer be exempt from IHT. All private pensions and most workplace schemes are defined contribution.

The changes mean “unused” pension savings could be taxed as part of someone’s estate if they exceed the IHT threshold. Unused funds are money in a pension pot that has not been used to claim an income, such as buying an annuity.

However, the insurer Legal & General says it surveyed 2,000 UK adults aged 50-plus earlier this year, and found misconceptions and confusion about annuities remained “widespread”.

For example, only 35% of respondents correctly identified a lifetime annuity as the retirement option that guaranteed an income for life. Meanwhile, 30% felt that annuities were too difficult to understand.

But L&G says: “Annuities are actually quite simple. They let you exchange some or all of your pension savings for a guaranteed income.”

However, it adds: “They are not right for everyone. Annuities generally cannot be changed once set up or cancelled after the cooling-off period.”

L&G has a myth-busting guide on its website .
