title: Sean Kelly: Here’s Why Pogačar Doesn’t Have to Fear Seixas Anytime Soon
author: sstokes
text:
Paul Seixas is seen as a likely successor to Tadej Pogačar. (Photo: Maarten Straetemans / Belga / AFP) (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS)

Paul Seixas has made remarkable progress this season, notching up eight wins in all, including a Tadej Pogačar -type dominance of Il Lombardia last weekend.

However although Seixas’ Cannibalesque ascent of the Civiglio saw him break the record Pogačar set four years ago on the same climb, and despite a stunning rate of improvement this season, experienced cycling analyst Sean Kelly feels the world number one shouldn’t lose sleep anytime soon.

Kelly spoke to Velo this week about the two riders and explained why he is believes Pogačar will have the edge for some time yet.

“If you had Pogačar there on Saturday, Seixas probably would have been able to stay with him once again,” he said, speaking of the hilly finale of Il Lombardia. “But then in the flat sprint he doesn’t have any chance, because Pogačar is very fast in a two-up sprint or a little group sprint.

“It’s the other quality that he’s got. As I said many times, Pogačar can do fecking everything.”

Seixas turned heads in Liège-Bastogne-Liège when the then 19-year-old was the only rider able to hold onto Pogačar when the UAE Emirates-XRG rider went all out on La Redoute.

He stayed with him to the summit and then began trading pulls with him afterward. The duo continued together out front until the defending champion put in a last-gasp surge on the climb of La Roche aux Faucons. That finally broke Seixas, but Pogačar admitted afterward that he had believed they’d reach the finish line together.

It’s incredibly rare for any rider to be able to cling on when Pogačar is going all out on a tough climb. It was an even more remarkable achievement for a 19-year-old second-year professional, and it highlighted the extraordinary talent the Frenchman has.

But Kelly insists that even if Seixas is able to remain with Pogačar, that’s only one part of the game.

“There’s no weakness with him where you can say, ‘oh yeah, we can get him on that one.’ They’re just not there. So I don’t think Pogačar is going to be worried.”

There will be some who will disagree with Kelly’s point. They will point to the large age gap between the two riders, a full eight years. They will note that Pogačar has just turned 28, an age when riders are in their prime, and note that it’s very often the time where performances start to plateau and then, a year or two later, start to decline.

Still, Kelly doesn’t think that will be an issue anytime soon. He argues Pogačar will remain the best rider in the sport as long as one thing is in place: motivation.

“Pogačar at 28, 29 or 30 – if mentally he’s hungry enough to do it, I don’t think there’s going to be a problem age-wise,” the former world number one said. “Pogačar definitely has another three or four top years left in him. But will he do four years? Will he have that focus, the mentality to continue on?

“We hear about these long term contracts and that, but in three years’ time, if Pogačar said after the Tour de France, ‘I’m finished, that’s it, I’m stopping at the end of this year,’ it wouldn’t surprise me.”

Pogačar’s ability to stay at the top level is one vital element in any speculation about their future tussles.

The other relates to the Frenchman himself. Kelly acknowledged that Seixas is forging new ground, being the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and also becoming the youngest rider to start the Tour de France in 89 years.

Those kinds of performances, plus Seixas’ stunning rate of improvement this year—remember, he had no pro wins at all prior to 2025, and now he has eight—lead many to assume that he will leap up another level in 2027.

Hold on, says Kelly. It’s not necessarily accurate to make such presumptions.

“It depends now where Seixas goes from here,” he explained. “Will he continue on improving? Is there much more improvement left in him? Or is he a very early developer, and the level he’s at now is pretty much the level he’s going to be at?

“Maybe that is going to be his best level.”

It seems unlikely that a talented young rider could stop improving, but Kelly believes an error was made this year. He explains what that was and how he thinks it might affect cycling’s most exciting young rider.

“I would be concerned that it was too young to do a Tour de France this year,” he said. “And also to ride it as he did, going for the general classification, every day being there in the battle. His potential might suffer because of doing the Tour de France too young.

“I would be concerned that a guy at 19, doing a Tour of France [as intensely] as they do it now, it could affect his performance next year, the year after. He mightn’t get that potential that would be there if he had been taken along at an easier level.”

Kelly mentions Laurent Fignon as a rider from his era who was incredibly good very young. The Frenchman won the Tour at 22 and 23 but, despite those incredible early performances, never won the race again. He missed out by eight seconds to Greg LeMond in 1989 and won the Giro that same year, but it’s fair to say that his early momentum didn’t lead to the dominance many had predicted.

To be clear, Kelly is wowed by Seixas. He does suggest that slightly sub-par performances by Isaac del Toro and Remco Evenepoel in Il Lombardia made the Frenchman look even better than he was but, nevertheless, he applauds his performance.

He also gives credit where credit is due for the year as a whole.

“You couldn’t but be impressed about the performances. We were hearing about the power outputs that he was doing in training,” he said. “We were hearing all that and then he comes to Pays Basques, the way he dominated there.

“The way he dominated the beginning of the year, that confirmed what we were hearing, what the French were talking him up about. And he’s confirmed all that through the year.…

title: The Best Pro Cyclists’ FTPs Are Even Higher Than You Thought
author: Will Tracy
text:
When Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney won atop Mont Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes this summer, we thought it was one of the best climbing performances in cycling history . Since then, more information has come out, not only confirming Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance, but putting it on the pedestal as the greatest climb in the history of women’s cycling.

We estimated Niewiadoma-Phinney’s output at 5.3w/kg for the duration of Mont Ventoux. But in a social media post, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s husband, Taylor, said that the actual output was closer to 5.6w/kg. This is due to the fact that Niewiadoma-Phinney rode into a headwind in the final third of the climb, and that her raw power output is relatively low, making her power-to-weight ratio even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney is one of a small group of riders in the women’s pro peloton who can probably hold 6w/kg for 10-20 minutes. These types of numbers were unfathomable a few years ago, but just like the men’s side of the sport, we have seen professional cycling progressing at a rapid rate. Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance on Mont Ventoux was one of those moments where we had to rewrite the power curve for women’s cycling. If you could hold 5w/kg for an hour in 2025, you could fight for the podium at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift. But in 2026, 5w/kg won’t even put you in the top five.

In this article, we’ll lay out the best women’s riders’ FTPs, and explain why it is their strength or weakness. Let’s start with none other than the Tour de France Femmes and world championship winner.

The last time that Demi Vollering posted power data publicly was in 2022, but her file from the 2021 Liège-Bastogne-Liège Femmes is still on Strava. The Dutchwoman pushed 362w (6.3w/kg) for 4min 34sec on La Redoute, and went on to take the win in a small group sprint. Since then, Vollering’s power data has disappeared, but we can make some educated guesses as to how much she’s improved.

Vollering finished second on Mont Ventoux, 1:16 behind Niewiadoma-Phinney in the queen stage of the TDFF. But she had attacked on the bottom slopes of the climb, pushing the pace and inadvertently setting up a perfect counterattack for Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering and Marlen Reusser were nearly two minutes behind Niewiadoma-Phinney with a few kilometers to go, but then Vollering put in a massive attack to close the gap by more than 30 seconds. That kind of acceleration is only possible when you’ve been riding well under threshold, suggesting that Vollering had plenty left in the tank while Niewiadoma-Phinney rode away solo.

Despite only pushing an estimated 5.1w/kg for the majority of Mont Ventoux, Vollering finished with such a burst that her actual FTP must be significantly higher. Based on our calculations, Vollering has an FTP of just over 300w, putting her at 5.3w/kg at an estimated weight of 57kg. That means that Vollering has a fantastic balance between raw power and w/kg. It’s why she can drop most riders on a climb, but she can also drop them on a shallow descent. She can solo to victory on the flats, and win a small group sprint with her raw power output. For her biggest rival at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, it is a completely different story.

At an estimated 49kg, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney is about 8kg lighter than Vollering, and more than 20kg lighter than Marlen Reusser. That creates a massive raw power discrepancy between the rivals, with few scenarios in Niewiadoma-Phinney’s favor. One of the only times that Niewiadoma-Phinney has the upper hand is on steep climbs. We saw this at the TDFF, when Niewiadoma-Phinney broke away on Mont Ventoux, and was able to follow Vollering’s attacks on a number of short and punchy climbs.

But as soon as they reach the descent or flat section of road, Niewiadoma-Phinney is immediately disadvantaged. We saw this clearly on stages 8 and 9 of this year’s Tour de France Femmes. Niewiadoma-Phinney was only a few seconds behind Vollering at the crest of a key climb, but then she would lose 20-30 seconds on the descent. These were shallow, non-technical descents of 3-5%, meaning that raw power and high speed would dominate.

But on the long and steep climb to Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio reigned supreme. The Pole broke away on the steepest section of the climb, building an insurmountable lead before the shallower and windier section of the course. At 49kg, she was giving away 50-100w compared to Vollering and Reusser, but that didn’t matter on a 9% gradient.

Niewiadoma-Phinney likely has the highest FTP in terms of watts per kilogram in women’s cycling. She reportedly did 5.6w/kg for 55 minutes on Mont Ventoux, which means her fresh numbers could be even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney – Mont Ventoux (UPDATED)

Steep Section to Chalet Reynard : 32:09 at 5.7w/kg (1,540 Vm/h)

In stark contrast to Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio is Marlen Reusser, one of the tallest and most powerful women in professional cycling. Standing at 1.8 meters tall, the Swiss rider weighs an estimated 70kg, meaning that she has more raw power than perhaps any other woman in the world. In fact, her estimated FTP of 370w is world class, regardless of gender.

Reusser was in the shape of her life at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, and she was riding into a podium spot before a final stage collapse in Nice. But before that, Reusser was following Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney on every piece of terrain. Short climbs, long climbs, technical descents, flats, and final sprints…Reusser was there every step of the way. She even won the 21-kilometer time trial in Dijon, putting 18 seconds into Vollering and over a minute into Niewiadoma-Phinney.…

title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
author: Kim Willsher in Paris
text:
Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers

Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.

In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).

Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.

Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.

“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris . “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”

After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”

If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.

Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.

The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe .

Gérôme Billois , a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.

“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.

“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.

“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”

The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.

Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.

Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.

“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.

“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”

She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”

The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.

France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.

In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.

Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.

“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.

In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.…

title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
author: Kat Wong with agencies
text:
Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.

Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico .

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.

Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.

Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.

The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.

Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.

The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.

They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.

The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.

Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.

He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
author: Kat Wong
text:
Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.

Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister, Mathias Cormann , is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25% , according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.

“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.

“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”

Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities.

He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.

But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.

Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation , would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.

He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.

“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.

“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”
